questions.stem: Drug X has a KD of 1 nM and drug Y a KD of 100 nM at the same receptor. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Y has 100 times higher affinity than X
options.B: X occupies half the receptors at a concentration 100 times lower than Y
options.C: X must have greater efficacy than Y
options.D: X must be a full agonist
options.E: Y reaches a higher maximal binding (Bmax)

questions.explanation: KD is the concentration for half-maximal binding; a lower KD means higher affinity, so X half-saturates at 1 nM vs 100 nM for Y. A: Reverses the relationship. C: Affinity says nothing about efficacy. D: Agonist vs antagonist isn't determined by KD. E: Bmax reflects receptor number, not the drug's KD.

questions.stem: At a receptor with significant constitutive activity, a drug reduces the response below the basal level, even with no agonist present. What is this drug?
questions.explanation: Inverse agonists have negative efficacy, returning constitutively active R# to Ri (e.g., cetirizine at H1). A: A full agonist raises the response to maximum. B: A partial agonist raises it to a submaximal ceiling. C: A neutral antagonist alone leaves basal activity unchanged. E: A physiological antagonist works through a different receptor.

questions.stem: In the presence of a fixed concentration of antagonist, the agonist's log dose–response curve shifts to the right in parallel, and the same maximal response is still reached. Which type of antagonist is this?
questions.explanation: Reversible competitive antagonists are surmountable: a parallel right shift with unchanged Emax. B: An irreversible antagonist lowers the maximum. C: A non-competitive antagonist depresses the slope and the maximum. D: A physiological antagonist acts through another receptor and doesn't produce a simple parallel shift at the same receptor. E: A chemical antagonist inactivates the drug itself.

questions.stem: A reversible competitive antagonist is present at a concentration equal to 4 × its KA. By how much must the agonist concentration be increased to restore the original response?
questions.explanation: Schild: dose ratio = [A]/KA + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5. A: 2-fold applies when [A] = KA. B: Forgets the +1. C: Subtracts 1 instead of adding it. D: Competitive reversible block is surmountable.

questions.stem: Epinephrine reverses histamine-induced bronchoconstriction in anaphylaxis. What type of antagonism is this?
questions.explanation: Two agonists produce opposing effects through different receptors (H1 vs β2): physiological antagonism. A: Chemical means the two drugs combine directly. B: Pharmacokinetic means changing histamine's concentration. D: Epinephrine doesn't compete at H1 receptors. E: Non-competitive antagonism blocks the chain beyond the same agonist's receptor.

questions.stem: For an agonist at cardiac β-adrenoceptors, the EC50 for the contractile response is much lower than the KD for binding. What does this indicate?

options.A: The agonist is a partial agonist
options.C: There is an inverse agonist present

questions.explanation: EC50 < KD means half-maximal response arrives before half the receptors are occupied: a receptor reserve (spare receptors). A: A partial agonist couldn't give the full response even at full occupancy. B: Irreversible binding isn't inferred from EC50 vs KD. C: An inverse agonist would reduce basal activity. E: Desensitization would raise the EC50.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man on chronic methadone maintenance is given buprenorphine in the emergency department for pain. Within minutes he develops yawning, rhinorrhea, piloerection, and abdominal cramps. What best explains this?

options.A: Buprenorphine is a full μ agonist and caused overdose
options.C: Buprenorphine is an inverse agonist at μ receptors
options.E: Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial μ agonist that displaced methadone

questions.explanation: As a partial agonist with high affinity, buprenorphine displaces the full agonist and gives less receptor activation, acting as an antagonist and precipitating withdrawal. A: Full-agonist overdose causes miosis and respiratory depression, not withdrawal. B: Enzyme induction takes days. C: It isn't classified as an inverse agonist. D: The signs are classic opioid withdrawal, not allergy.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man stops his long-term metoprolol abruptly because he ran out. Two days later he has palpitations, BP 175/100, and chest pain at rest. What is the mechanism?

options.A: Downregulation of β receptors during treatment
options.C: Upregulation of β receptors during chronic blockade

questions.explanation: Chronic blockade upregulates β receptors; when the antagonist is removed, normal catecholamine levels act on excess receptors → overshoot (rebound tachycardia, hypertension, angina). Hence tapering. A: Downregulation follows chronic agonist exposure, not blockade. B: Tachyphylaxis is a fading response during repeated dosing. D: Hypersensitivity is immune-mediated. E: More enzyme would reduce catecholamine effects.

questions.stem: Phenoxybenzamine is given before surgery for pheochromocytoma. A day after the last dose the drug is barely detectable in plasma, yet α-blockade persists. Why?

options.A: It is a reversible competitive antagonist with very high affinity
options.B: It binds covalently, so recovery needs synthesis of new receptors
options.C: It has an active metabolite with a long half-life
options.D: It is a non-competitive antagonist acting beyond the receptor

questions.explanation: Irreversible (covalent) antagonists act until receptors are replaced, so their duration depends on receptor turnover rather than drug elimination. A: A reversible block would fade as plasma levels fall. C: The block persists because the receptors themselves are inactivated, not because of a metabolite. D: Phenoxybenzamine binds the α-receptor itself; non-competitive antagonists (verapamil) act beyond it. E: Up-regulation would increase, not block, the response.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with a morphine overdose wakes after IV naloxone. Ninety minutes later, with no further opioid use, he is drowsy again with a respiratory rate of 6/min. What best explains this?

options.A: Naloxone is cleared faster than morphine, so morphine regains the receptors
options.B: Naloxone is a partial agonist that adds to respiratory depression
options.C: Tachyphylaxis to naloxone at μ receptors
options.D: Naloxone binds irreversibly and then releases morphine
options.E: Up-regulation of μ receptors by naloxone

questions.explanation: When an agonist and an antagonist compete, concentration decides: as the shorter-acting naloxone is cleared, morphine reoccupies μ receptors and respiratory depression returns. B: Naloxone is a pure antagonist with no intrinsic activity. C: Tachyphylaxis is a fading response to repeated agonist doses, not antagonist clearance. D: Naloxone is a reversible competitive antagonist. E: Up-regulation needs chronic blockade and wouldn't cause respiratory depression.
